context: area network · ducts and chambers are the bulk; cable blowing, splicing and OTDR testing are fast

brief.intro: New to this project type? A telecom network is mostly a civil job with a short technical finish. Ducts and chambers are laid along every street; fibre cable is then blown or pulled through them, spliced in closures and cabinets, and tested end to end with an OTDR. Finally the active equipment in the exchange or point-of-presence is powered and the service is switched on. The ducts take months; blowing, splicing and testing take weeks. The ducts are shallow, so telecom is one of the last utilities laid in a road — but its road-crossing ducts must still be in before the road base, and the building that houses the equipment needs power and cooling before anything can be lit.

glossary.plain: the levels of the network, from the main cable down to the cable into each building.
a small tube inside a duct through which a thin fibre cable is blown with compressed air.
installing fibre by floating it through the duct on a stream of air — fast and gentle on the cable.
joining two fibres by melting them together; the loss of each splice is measured.
the sealed box in a chamber that protects a group of splices.
optical distribution frame — the rack where fibres end and are patched in the equipment room.
an instrument that sends light down a fibre and shows the position and loss of every splice and fault.
the active unit in the exchange and the passive device that shares one fibre among many customers (in FTTH).
point of presence — the building or room that houses the active equipment.

must_get_right: Treat it as a civil programme: metres of duct and number of chambers per day set the duration. Sequence it after the deeper utilities and before kerbs and paving.
Put road-crossing ducts in before the road base, with spare ducts — crossings are the expensive part to add later.
Prove every duct (rod and mandrel) and leave a draw rope before the cable crew arrives; blocked ducts are the usual cause of delay at the cable stage.
The equipment room needs permanent power, batteries and cooling before active equipment is installed; that readiness, and the operator's acceptance of OTDR results, are the end milestones.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by network area (cabinet or splitter area) and route section, so each area shows ducts complete, cable installed, spliced, tested and activated.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar; works in live roads may be restricted to off-peak hours. Splicing and testing are not weather-dependent once chambers are dry.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Road-crossing ducts → trench, ducts and chambers → duct proving → cable blowing → splicing → OTDR test → activation. In parallel the POP building is completed, powered and cooled, then active equipment is installed. The critical path runs through the last duct section released, or the POP power supply.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Roads and other utilities release the telecom corridor in the planned order; the operator approves the design and accepts test results within the assumed review time; permanent power is available at the POP.

sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Telecom ducts are shallow and laid late, among finished utilities. Chambers must fit between other services and driveways. Fibre work needs clean, dry chambers.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: ducts damaged or blocked by later works, late road release, late POP power, and fibres failing the loss budget at the OTDR stage. Contingency is held before activation.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by network area and route section; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the ducting, cabling and splicing teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
